summary: Describes RTP, a protocol for carrying real-time data such as audio and video over unicast or multicast networks. It adds sequencing and timing information so receivers can play media back smoothly, and it comes with a companion control protocol. It was replaced by RFC 3550.

plainLanguage.summary: RTP is the header that makes live media work over an unreliable network. It labels each packet with what it holds, which packet it is, when the sound or picture was sampled and who sent it, so the receiver can play the media at the right speed and notice what is missing. A companion protocol, RTCP, reports back what each receiver is actually getting.

subtitle: Carrying live audio and video over a network that may lose, delay or reorder packets.

tldr.problem: Live media needs to be played out on schedule, but the underlying network loses packets, reorders them and delays them by varying amounts, and it gives no guarantee about delivery.
tldr.mechanism: RTP adds a fixed 12-octet header to each packet carrying a payload type, a sequence number, a timestamp and a source identifier, and pairs it with RTCP, a periodic control protocol that reports what receivers are getting.
tldr.outcome: The headers let receivers rebuild the sender's timing, detect losses and play out the media smoothly, without the protocol itself promising delivery. RFC 1889 was obsoleted by RFC 3550.

today: RFC 1889 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 3550.

sections.title: What RTP Is For
sections.content:
RTP provides end-to-end delivery services for data with real-time characteristics, such as interactive audio and video. Those services include payload type identification, sequence numbering, timestamping and delivery monitoring. Applications typically run RTP on top of UDP to make use of its multiplexing and checksum services, but RTP may be used with other suitable underlying network or transport protocols. RTP supports data transfer to multiple destinations using multicast distribution if the underlying network provides it.

RTP itself provides no mechanism to ensure timely delivery or any other quality-of-service guarantee, and relies on lower-layer services for that. It does not guarantee delivery and does not prevent out-of-order delivery, nor does it assume the underlying network is reliable. The sequence numbers in RTP let the receiver reconstruct the sender's packet sequence, and they may also be used to place a packet correctly, for example in video decoding, without decoding packets in order.

RTP is primarily designed for multi-participant multimedia conferences but is not limited to that. Storage of continuous data, interactive distributed simulation, active badge, and control and measurement applications may also find it applicable.

The document defines two closely linked parts: RTP itself, which carries data with real-time properties, and RTCP, the control protocol, which monitors the quality of service and conveys information about the participants. RTCP is described as a protocol framework that is deliberately not complete, intended to be tailored through modifications and additions to the headers as needed rather than through a general option mechanism. A complete specification for a particular application also needs a profile specification, which defines payload type codes and their mapping to payload formats, and payload format specifications, which define how a particular payload is carried in RTP.
sections.plainLanguage: RTP does not promise that your data arrives. It adds just enough information to each packet for the receiver to work out what it missed and when to play each piece. It is meant to be adjusted to the application rather than kept general, so an audio application and a video application each get the header they need.

sections.title: Sessions, Sources and Roles
sections.content:
An RTP session is the association among a set of participants. For each participant the session is defined by a pair of destination transport addresses, one network address plus a port pair for RTP and RTCP. The pair may be common to all participants, as with IP multicast, or different for each, as with individual unicast addresses plus a common port pair. In a multimedia session each medium is carried in a separate RTP session with its own RTCP packets, and the sessions are told apart by different port pairs and different multicast addresses.

A synchronization source, or SSRC, is the source of a stream of RTP packets, identified by a 32-bit numeric identifier carried in the RTP header so that the identifier does not depend on the network address. All packets from one synchronization source share a single timing and sequence number space, so a receiver groups packets by synchronization source for playback. The identifier is chosen at random with the intent of being globally unique within a session, and every implementation must be prepared to detect and resolve collisions. If a source changes its transport address it must also choose a new identifier, so that it is not read as a looped source.

A contributing source, or CSRC, is a source that has contributed to the combined stream produced by an RTP mixer. The mixer inserts the list of contributing SSRC identifiers into the header of each packet it produces, which lets a receiver show who is currently talking even though all the packets carry the mixer's own SSRC.

An end system generates the content or consumes it. A mixer is an intermediate system that receives packets from one or more sources, possibly changes the data format, combines them and forwards a new packet, making timing adjustments because the inputs are not synchronised, and becomes the synchronization source for everything it sends. A translator is an intermediate system that forwards packets with their synchronization source identifier intact, such as a device that converts encodings without mixing, a replicator from multicast to unicast, or a firewall filter. A monitor receives the RTCP packets and estimates the current quality of service for distribution monitoring, fault diagnosis and long-term statistics.
sections.plainLanguage: A session is a group of participants identified by an address and two port numbers, and each medium in a conference gets its own session. Each sender is tagged with a random 32-bit number so that receivers can keep its packets apart and play them in step. A mixer combines several senders into one stream and adds a list of who contributed; a translator passes packets on without changing who sent them.

sections.title: The RTP Header
sections.content:
The fixed header is twelve octets long and is followed by a list of contributing sources when a mixer has inserted one. It carries: version, 2 bits, which is two in this specification; padding, 1 bit, set when the packet ends with padding octets, the last of which counts how many to ignore; extension, 1 bit, set when a header extension follows; CSRC count, 4 bits, giving the number of contributing source identifiers that follow; marker, 1 bit, whose meaning a profile defines, intended for significant events such as frame boundaries; payload type, 7 bits, identifying the format of the payload; sequence number, 16 bits, which increments by one per data packet and lets the receiver detect loss and restore order; timestamp, 32 bits, reflecting the sampling instant of the first octet of the payload; and SSRC, 32 bits, identifying the synchronization source.

The sequence number's initial value is random, so that known-plaintext attacks on encryption are harder even if the source itself does not encrypt, because the packets may pass through a translator that does. The timestamp reflects the sampling instant of the first octet in the packet, taken from a clock that increases monotonically and linearly in time so that synchronization and jitter calculations are possible; its resolution must be fine enough for the accuracy wanted, and one tick per video frame is typically not sufficient. If packets are generated periodically, the nominal sampling instant from the sampling clock is used rather than a reading of the system clock, so a block of 160 sampling periods raises the timestamp by 160 whether it is sent or dropped as silence. The initial timestamp value is random, as for the sequence number.

The CSRC list holds 0 to 15 identifiers of 32 bits each, and if there are more than 15 contributing sources only 15 may be identified. A profile may redefine the octet holding the marker bit and payload type, and may define extra fixed fields after the SSRC field, while profile-independent monitors and recorders still process only the first twelve octets. If functionality turns out to be needed across all profiles, a new version of RTP should be defined.
sections.plainLanguage: The header is twelve octets and does four jobs at once: it says what the payload is, numbers the packets so gaps can be spotted, records when the media was sampled so it can be played on time, and names the sender. The sequence number and the timestamp both start at random values, which makes an attacker's job harder if the stream is later encrypted.

sections.title: The RTCP Control Protocol
sections.content:
RTCP is based on the periodic transmission of control packets to all participants in the session, using the same distribution mechanism as the data packets. It performs four functions. The primary one is to provide feedback on the quality of the data distribution, which is an integral part of the RTP role as a transport protocol and is related to flow and congestion control; the feedback may be useful for controlling adaptive encodings, and experiments with IP multicasting showed it is critical to get feedback from receivers to diagnose faults in the distribution. Second, RTCP carries a persistent transport-level identifier for an RTP source, the canonical name or CNAME, because the SSRC identifier may change if a conflict is discovered or a program is restarted, and receivers need the CNAME to associate multiple data streams from one participant in related sessions, for example to synchronise audio and video. Third, because the first two functions require every participant to send RTCP packets, the rate must be controlled for RTP to scale to a large number of participants; by having each participant send to all the others, each can independently observe the number of participants and use it to calculate the sending rate. Fourth, an optional function is to convey minimal session control information, such as participant identification for display in the user interface.

RTCP packets have a fixed part similar to that of RTP data packets, followed by structured elements that vary by type and always end on a 32-bit boundary. Multiple RTCP packets may be concatenated with no separators into a compound packet sent in one packet of the lower layer protocol. All RTCP packets must be sent in a compound packet of at least two individual packets. The first packet must always be a report packet, even if no data has been sent or received, in which case an empty receiver report is sent, and even if the only other packet is a BYE. An SDES packet containing a CNAME item must be included in each compound packet. Other packet types may follow in any order, except that BYE should be last for a given source.

Because the control traffic is not self-limiting, the sending rate must be scaled down as the session grows. The suggested fraction of the session bandwidth allocated to RTCP is 5%, and all participants must use the same constants so that they calculate the same interval. The interval must be greater than a minimum of 5 seconds, and it is varied randomly over the range [0.5, 1.5] times the calculated interval to avoid all the participants synchronising.
sections.plainLanguage: RTCP is the side channel that tells everyone how the session is going. It reports packet loss and timing back to the senders, and it carries a stable name for each participant so receivers can link audio and video from the same person. It also lets each participant work out how often to speak without anyone having to tell it. The rate shrinks as the session grows, so the control traffic stays a small share of the bandwidth.

sections.title: Translators and Mixers
sections.content:
Intermediate systems can sit between the participants of a session. A translator forwards RTP packets with their synchronization source identifier intact, and may change the payload format. A mixer receives packets from one or more sources, possibly changes the data format, combines the packets and forwards a new packet; because the timing among multiple inputs is not generally synchronised, the mixer makes timing adjustments among the streams and generates its own timing for the combined stream. All data packets originating from a mixer are identified as having the mixer as their synchronization source.

Because a mixer combines several sources, it must also handle their control packets. The RFC describes how translators and mixers process RTCP: a translator forwards the control packets of the sources it forwards, and a mixer must rewrite the source descriptions in the packets it forwards, since it is now the source of the data it sends. Cascaded mixers, where one mixer's output feeds another, are also described. The RFC notes that translators and mixers should combine individual RTCP packets from the multiple sources they forward into one compound packet whenever feasible, in order to amortize the packet overhead.
sections.plainLanguage: A translator changes a stream without changing who sent it, for example converting the codec or copying a multicast stream to one receiver. A mixer combines several streams into one, so it becomes the sender of everything it emits and has to rewrite the control information too. Both are told to bundle the control packets they forward into as few packets as possible to save overhead.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
Lower layer protocols may eventually provide all the security services that might be wanted for RTP applications, including authentication, integrity and confidentiality, and services have recently been specified for IP. Because the need for a confidentiality service is well established in the audio and video applications expected to use RTP, a confidentiality service is defined for use with RTP and RTCP until lower layer services are available. Key distribution and certificates are outside the scope of this document.

Confidentiality is achieved by encryption. When encryption is desired, all the octets to be encapsulated in a single lower-layer packet are encrypted as a unit. For RTCP a 32-bit random number is prepended to the unit before encryption to deter known plaintext attacks; for RTP no prefix is required, because the sequence number and timestamp fields are initialised with random offsets. The default algorithm is DES in cipher block chaining mode, with padding to a multiple of 8 octets indicated as for the padding bit, and a zero initialisation vector because random values are supplied in the RTP header or by the random prefix. The presence of encryption and the correct key are confirmed by the receiver through header or payload validity checks.

Authentication and message integrity are not defined in this specification, since these services would not be directly feasible without a key management infrastructure. It is expected that they will be provided by lower layer protocols in the future.
sections.plainLanguage: RTP can encrypt the media, using DES in CBC mode by default, with a random number in front of each encrypted control packet to make known plaintext attacks harder. It does not define authentication or message integrity, because those need a way to manage keys, which the RFC leaves to lower layers. Key distribution and certificates are out of scope.

fields.name: Version (V)
fields.desc: Identifies the version of RTP. This specification defines version two.

fields.name: Padding (P)
fields.desc: Set when the packet ends with padding octets that are not part of the payload.

fields.name: Extension (X)
fields.desc: Set when one header extension follows the fixed header.

fields.name: CSRC count (CC)
fields.desc: The number of contributing source identifiers that follow.

fields.name: Marker (M)
fields.desc: Defined by a profile; intended to mark significant events such as frame boundaries.

fields.name: Payload type (PT)
fields.desc: Identifies the format of the RTP payload.

fields.name: Sequence number
fields.desc: Increments by one per data packet; used to detect loss and restore order.

fields.name: Timestamp
fields.desc: The sampling instant of the first octet of the payload.
